newsitem.title: CANADA: Westcoast applies for 25 percent toll hike.
newsitem.headline: Westcoast applies for 25 percent toll hike.

text.p: Gas pipeline operator Westcoast Energy Inc said Wednesday it filed a rate application with Canada's National Energy Board seeking an increase of about 25 percent in the typical toll for 1997.
Westcoast said that while it has filed the application "it remains hopeful that it can negotiate a settlement with its shippers."
In the toll application, Westcoast said it proposes an incentive-based method for setting certain components of the cost of service for transmission facilities for five years to 2001.

Westcoast said its application relects an increase in its rate base to about C$2.3 billion with an overall deemed 35 percent common equity component of the rate base and an after-tax rate of return on common equity of 11.25 percent.
It also incorporates increases in depreciation rates and other cost of service increases that result in a revenue requirement about 12 percent higher than 1996.
This combined with a reduction in contracted firm service levels results in an incrase of about 25 percent in the typical toll, Westcoast said.
Westcoast said it wants longer term contracts. "The current one-year contract renewals are causing distortions in the marketplace," it said.

An increase in gas prices in northeastern British Columbia over the past two months also improves prospects that the company will be able to negotiate the longer term arrangements it wants, Westcoast said.

The incentive-toll application contemplates fixing annual operating and maintenance expenses over the five-year period based on the 1996 approved level adjusted for inflation and productivity savings.
Additions to its rate base arising from minor capital additions would also be fixed by formula over the five years.
The application includes 1997 tolls for gathering and processing which incorporates an optional gas-price sensitive toll for gathring and processing services.

The new toll, which could be selected by customers as an alternative to standard tolls, involves a discount to the standard toll with a variable surcharge adjustment based on an index of actual gas prices for each month in 1997 compared to a base period.
Westcoast said it expects to file by year end a further proposal for an incentive-based regime for its gathering and processing facilities in northeast British Columbia.

The proposal will include a four-year transition period from 1998 to 2001. The proposal would include an option to tie a portion of the tolls to commodity prices, structuring tolls to meet specific customer needs and delivering lower tolls through longer term contracts.
Westcoast previously announced that certain shippers who source their gas around Fort Nelson would not renew their firm gathering and processing services agreements effective Nov 1.
In its toll application, Westcoast said it forecast a 10 percent decrease in firm contracted gathering service and a 17 percent decrease in firm contracted processing service.
Other shipers have said they would not renew part of their firm transportation service on the northern and southern segments of the transmission mainline effective November 1997.

In its toll application, Westcoast forecast that much of the non-renewals of firm service would be replaced with new firm service contracts. The result would be a three percent drop on the northern segment and no drop on the southern segment.
Westcoast said the reduction in contracted level of firm service accounts for about half of its requested 1997 toll increase.
A reorganization of the company's pipeline and field services division announced in August is expected to result in a 25 percent staff cut and restructuring costs of about C$29 million.
Westcoast expects it to lead to cost savings in 1997 but did not specify the amount.
-- Reuters Vancouver Bureau (604) 664-7314
